Lim Wee Peng, medical director of Parkway Shenton, said there was a noticeable uptick in patients with sore throat, runny nose, eye irritation, as well as asthma and flare-ups in patients with pre-existing asthma and hay fever during that period. “The key lesson from January to March is that even short-duration, moderate-level haze generates a measurable clinical signal,” he said. The Parkway Shenton clinics have sufficient stock for respiratory medications including inhalers and antihistamines. “Our doctors are briefed on the interaction between heat stress and poor air quality — the combination is more dangerous than either alone, because haze discourages outdoor hydration breaks while heat drives up respiratory demand,” Lim added . Shabana Begum is a correspondent, with a focus on environment and science, at The Straits Times.

title: Government will do studies on rich marine biodiversity before western island reclamation
environment_keywords: environmental, biodiversity, conservation, ecosystem, marine biodiversity
article_text: Prime Minister Lawrence Wong had announced that an island for industry, energy and defence needs would be reclaimed in coming decades by combining several southern islands. Published Aug 25, 2026, 05:00 AM Updated Aug 31, 2026, 12:53 PM SINGAPORE – Recognising the biodiversity value of the western islands and its surrounding waters, the authorities are carefully studying plans for future reclamation, and will be conducting technical studies as well as engaging stakeholders . This comes as scientists and nature groups have stressed the need for comprehensive studies and public consultation before reclamation begins because they believe the works will cause irreversible loss to the mature habitats in the area. A spokesman for the Ministry of National Development (MND) told The Straits Times: “As part of the planning process, the Government will be conducting technical studies to inform the development plans, including the reclamation profile. “These studies include feasibility studies, site investigations and surveys, as well as engineering and environmental studies, to better understand the various development possibilities and their preliminary impact on areas like biodiversity and hydrodynamics.” Eleven scientists and nature groups spoke to ST in the wake of the announcement of the planned reclamation at the 2026 National Day Rally. Prime Minister Lawrence Wong had announced that an island for industry, energy and defence needs would be reclaimed in coming decades by combining several southern islands. The intertidal habitats for various islands and surrounding reefs which could fall within the potential reclamation area cover about 592.8ha, according to data from the National Parks Board’s Southern Islands Biodiversity Survey. This is larger than the resort island of Sentosa, and makes up more than half the intertidal areas of the Southern Islands. Huang Danwei, director of the National Institute for Marine and Ocean Sciences, pointed out that reefs in Pulau Hantu and Pulau Semakau date back about 8,000 years. “The area highlighted for potential reclamation is a very large one, containing many sensitive marine habitats and ecosystems that have high value for climate mitigation, ecological connectivity, science and potential medicines,” he said, warning that Singapore will lose many of these functions if the entire area undergoes land reclamation. The mega-project could impact some of the most significant and valuable marine habitats in the Southern Islands, where nearly all of Singapore’s remaining natural coral reefs are found, the researchers said. Acknowledging the strategic need backing the reclamation, scientists and nature groups called for the protection of as many of these habitats and their species as possible, given their immense ecological value. Huang noted that the coral reefs of Pulau Hantu, Pulau Semakau and others in the area have shown how these natural habitats can persist even in the face of human activity, having recovered following global-scale coral bleaching events in 1998, 2010, 2016 and 2024. “There is no mitigation for reefs lost by direct burial for land reclamation,” he said. “Corals that can be transplanted are a few months or even years old, but they will not come close to restoring the ecosystem functions and services of coral reefs built over eight millennia.” Chou Loke Ming, emeritus professor at the National University of Singapore’s Department of Biological Sciences, believes that mature marine habitats like reefs, seagrass and mangroves qualify as natural heritage sites. These have consistently served the ecosystem in valuable ways, such as by acting as nurseries supporting fish populations and absorbing planet-warming carbon dioxide. The veteran marine scientist called for a new mindset on reclamation, where Singapore works towards building with nature instead of at the expense of it. For instance, the reclamation boundary could be made flexible to avoid burying most of these habitats, he suggested. Marine scientists and other stakeholders had proposed in the 2018 Singapore Blue Plan that Pulau Semakau, Pulau Hantu and Pulau Jong, together with other nearby reefs, be designated as a marine reserve . The proposal was not taken up. Marine biologist Zeehan Jaafar, lead editor of the plan, said the connected reef-mangrove-seagrass coastal systems at Pulau Semakau are no longer observed anywhere else in Singapore . Coral reefs have persisted on and near the landfill island despite development, with research done to understand why and how they continue to exist . She noted that the affected areas rank among the most studied marine sites globally, and said their loss will take away long-term insights into coastal system processes. “These areas are important to further understand our marine biodiversity and coastal ecological processes, especially as the biodiversity has been resilient in the face of increasing marine urbanisation,” she said. Jani Tanzil, facility director for St John’s Island National Marine Laboratory, noted that these spaces are valuable, as Singapore’s marine ecosystems sit at the confluence of waters like the South China Sea and Java Sea, making them a nature corridor that helps connect biodiversity and fisheries in the region. Tanzil and marine conservationist Ria Tan highlighted the role that the affected area plays as a “mother site” that provides genetic material to sustain nearby ecosystems beyond its boundaries. Said Tanzil: “ We must still consider all options. Studies and solutions must be comprehensive, even if it means challenging how development is done.” Tridacna crocea, commonly known as the burrowing giant clam or boring giant clam, among other corals seen during an intertidal survey led by marine conservationist Ria Tan at Pulau Hantu on July 31. Neo Mei Lin, a senior research fellow at St John’s Island National Marine Laboratory, noted that 80 per cent to 90 per cent of the wild populations of giant clams that she studies exist in the potentially affected areas. “The astronomical loss of marine habitats and its biodiversity is expected to be more devastating than the past island reclamation projects,” she said. Nature groups similarly stressed the need for the careful development of these spaces, which are key educational and recreational sites. The chairman of Nature Society Singapore’s marine conservation group, Lester Tan, said that the islands function as vital outdoor classrooms and living laboratories. “Losing these accessible areas means losing the exact spaces where we cultivate the next generation of conservationists and build the genuine public appreciation necessary to sustain our national conservation goals,” he said. Tan called for detailed environmental studies to guide this development, as well as for the Government to adopt a strict marine spatial zoning strategy that would identify and preserve the most resilient core reefs. Likewise, a spokesman for the Ichthyological Society of Singapore said the society founded by youth hopes the area will be rigorously surveyed to catalogue the rich biodiversity slated for development. He said: “Transparency is a must to ensure that the youth feel like they have a stake in their future.” The MND spokesperson said that stakeholders will be engaged to listen to their inputs before studies and work commence, with their feedback carefully considered. “Their knowledge and expertise will help inform the studies, assess potential biodiversity impact and identify measures to avoid, minimise and mitigate impacts where possible.”

title: Western island reclamation will create space for industries, low-carbon energy sources: Analysts
environment_keywords: environment, environmental, sustainability, hydrogen, low-carbon energy, pollution
article_text: Analysts said the new island would allow Singapore to design from scratch an integrated hub involving a range of low-carbon energy sources that can support Jurong Island. Published Aug 24, 2026, 09:35 PM Updated Aug 25, 2026, 10:16 AM SINGAPORE - The reclamation of a new western island will create a space for industries and power-related infrastructure that can tap the sea, and benefit from proximity to Jurong Island and the need for greater distance from residential areas, analysts said. At the National Day Rally on Aug 23, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong had outlined plans to form a new island south of energy and chemicals hub Jurong Island in the coming decades for industry, energy and defence needs, by merging islands such as Pulau Semakau, Pulau Bukom and Pulau Sudong. Analysts told The Straits Times that the new island would allow Singapore to design from scratch an integrated hub involving a range of low-carbon energy sources that can support Jurong Island, boosting the nation’s long-term energy security by creating space to accommodate technology that may become feasible only in the longer term. Nuclear energy infrastructure is one of the possible options among a host of low-carbon energy sources that can be sited on the island, they said. That said, they cautioned against seeing the deployment of nuclear energy as the aim of the reclamation, stressing that Singapore has yet to make a decision on the power source, which it is exploring as a low-carbon alternative, and noting the need for more detailed studies. Matthew Chew, nuclear competency and strategy lead at engineering consultancy HY, said that the new island would give Singapore the long-term physical space to accommodate technologies and energy systems that may not yet be commercially mature, but could become critical over the next decades. “Singapore could design the island as an integrated energy hub where gas, low-carbon fuels, electricity imports, storage, renewables and potentially nuclear eventually operate together,” he said. Tan-Soo Jie Sheng, director of the Institute for Environment and Sustainability at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy, noted that while western Singapore has a large industrial footprint, much of that land is already committed to existing uses. “Hence, what Singapore needs is sufficiently large, contiguous sites that can accommodate the new industries and energy infrastructure it may need several decades from now.” He added that offshore land also provides direct maritime access and space to build large-scale and difficult-to-site energy infrastructure from scratch, a common constraint for Singapore’s energy ambitions. Said Tan-Soo: “These characteristics could make it particularly suitable for activities that are land- or energy-intensive, require port access, or benefit from greater physical buffers. “Possibilities include next-generation energy and chemical industries, hydrogen- and ammonia-related activities, advanced manufacturing, and large-scale energy infrastructure.” Sing Tien Foo, NUS Business School’s provost chair professor of real estate, said the offshore island will prepare Singapore for the next wave of industrialisation, for which it will need to build a sufficient land bank in advance to attract investment in these greener, high-value-add industries. He said: “New industries that require massive infrastructure investment, are to be segregated from high-density residential housing estates, and will require intensive energy and water resources, are ideal on the island. By isolating these advanced and precision manufacturing risks, they could also protect against other types of human risks, including fire and pollution.” Tan-Soo noted that, fundamentally, Singapore does not know what the most important industries will be in 2050 or 2070, just as planners of the past did not know the scale of today’s demand for data centres and digital infrastructure, and the new site would offer flexibility. He added that offshore land also provides direct maritime access and the opportunity to build highly specialised infrastructure from scratch. In addition, the new island potentially helps Singapore address a constraint common to several of these pathways by providing sufficient and suitable land for large-scale and difficult-to-site energy infrastructure. Strategically, the move to form a second energy island beside Jurong will build resilience for Singapore’s energy system, said Marsh Asia’s energy and power leader, Benjamin Chang. He said: “Singapore’s energy security strategy has always been about creating options before you need them.” Chew said several factors could make the offshore industrial site a candidate for nuclear energy. These include access to seawater that can reduce the distance needed to convey water to cool nuclear power plants, as well as giving the land-constrained city-state more flexibility without locking up a major parcel on the mainland, he said, citing how nuclear power can represent a commitment of land for potentially 60 years or more. Analysts said that proximity to the Singapore Armed Forces could confer greater security, but there could be trade-offs. “The colocation of SAF on the island could also enhance security and protect valuable manufacturing plants from potential intrusion by imposing strict controls on access from unrelated parties and by establishing military zones that reduce the risk of sabotage or drone incursions. “This mirrors the existing model on Jurong Island, where strict access controls and security protocols protect high-value petrochemical and energy facilities. SAF proximity would reinforce the new island’s role as a secure, strategic node for Singapore’s future energy system,” said Sing. Chu Jian, a professor at NTU and its president’s chair in civil engineering, pointed out that while the military runway on Pulau Sudong could make the future development much easier to plan, there could also be restrictions on construction activities, such as height controls. Experts cautioned that use of the reclaimed island could mean navigating complex hurdles such as sea-level rise, emergency access and environmental impacts given its scale. Said NUS’ Energy Studies Institute senior research fellow Kim Jeong Won: “Significant investment would be needed for land reclamation, transport links, utility networks and grid connections, potentially making offshore generation more expensive than developing existing sites.”

title: PSI or PM2.5? What air quality measures should I refer to when there is haze?
environment_keywords: environment, haze, air quality, forest fires
article_text: A hazy city skyline as seen from Gardens by the Bay at 4.50pm on Aug 24. Published Aug 24, 2026, 09:10 PM Updated Aug 25, 2026, 10:14 AM SINGAPORE - The spectre of haze loomed over Singapore on Aug 24 , as the Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) in the central region inched ever closer to unhealthy levels. The 24-hour PSI reading was 98 at 9pm, just shy of 101, which indicates unhealthy air. For weeks, Sumatra and Kalimantan have been ablaze with forest and land fires fuelled by a super El Nino. How badly Singapore is affected hinges on wind direction. The Straits Times explains how local air quality readings should be used to plan outdoor activities. Haze and worsening air quality are shown through two readings on the National Environment Agency’s (NEA) website: the 24-hour Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) and the one-hour PM2.5 readings. Both measures serve different functions. During hazy periods, the one-hour PM2.5 – an indicator of fine micro-pollutants in the air – is what you should be watching because it points to current air quality. PM2.5 levels should be checked immediately before outdoor activities, such as going jogging or walking your dog. PM2.5 refers to micro-pollutants found in smoke haze from Indonesian forest fires. These particles – 30 times smaller than the width of a strand of hair – can get lodged deep in the lungs and enter the bloodstream. On the afternoon of Aug 24, the one-hour PM2.5 readings reached elevated levels in the central and east regions, at 56ug/m3 and above. PM2.5 values can be volatile and tend to fluctuate over the day, especially during haze. PM2.5 is the dominant pollutant during periods of transboundary haze, and has the most influence over the 24-hour PSI readings. The 24-hour PSI is computed based on the daily average concentration of six pollutants, including PM2.5, sulphur dioxide, carbon monoxide and ozone. The calculations are done based on readings from the past 24 hours. It is an index to provide easily understandable information about daily levels of air quality. Haze has descended when the PSI crosses 100, reaching unhealthy levels. During a haze episode, the National Environment Agency will issue a third air quality measure called the 24-hour PSI forecast. Not to be confused with the 24-hour PSI, the PSI forecast indicates what the air quality is expected to be in the next 24 hours and can be used to plan activities ahead of time. In a nutshell, during haze, people should refer to the PM2.5 values if they want to go outdoors within the hour, and refer to the PSI forecast if they are planning an outdoor activity the next day. During haze, if the PM2.5 readings are high – between 151ug/m3 and 250ug/m3 – people should avoid strenuous outdoor activities for the next hour. Vulnerable people – who include seniors, pregnant women, children and patients with lung and heart disease – should avoid all outdoor activities. These are outlined in the personal guide published on NEA’s website. Hazy conditions seen from Ang Mo Kio facing eastern Singapore on Aug 24. N95 masks are not needed for short periods of exposure, such as commuting to work. These masks are recommended under certain conditions, such as when a healthy person must be outdoors for several hours when the air quality is in the hazardous range, with a PSI reading of over 300. The authorities have said that national N95 mask stockpiles are sufficient. When the outdoor air quality appears to be worsening, close doors and windows. If the air-conditioner draws in unfiltered air from outside, close the outdoor air intake opening. Portable air purifiers can also be used to further improve indoor air. When planning for outdoor activities the next day, refer to the 24-hour PSI forecast and accompanying health advisory. When air quality is forecast to remain unhealthy at 101 and above, healthy individuals should reduce prolonged and strenuous outdoor activities. Seniors, pregnant women and children should minimise prolonged outdoor exertion, and those with lung and heart disease should avoid such activities. For healthy folk, continuous exposure to unhealthy air over a few days could cause eye, nose and throat irritation. They will resolve on their own in most cases. A hazy Jurong East skyline at 5.53pm on Aug 24. Lee Joon Loong, medical director of Paddington Medical Clinic, reminds patients with asthma to keep their reliever inhalers readily available and ensure that their inhalers are not expired and are being used correctly. Similarly, patients with hay fever should make sure that their antihistamines or nasal sprays are readily available and use them if their symptoms flare up. “Patients should seek medical review early if their symptoms are worsening rather than waiting until they become severely breathless,” said Lee. Shabana Begum is a correspondent, with a focus on environment and science, at The Straits Times.

title: Dung beetles bring poo-sitive news about animals in Central Catchment Nature Reserve
environment_keywords: environment, environmental, greenhouse gases, biodiversity, conservation, ecosystem, wildlife
article_text: NTU research fellow Ong Xin Rui (left) and associate professor Eleanor Slade with specimens of local dung beetles. There are more than 25 known local dung beetle species in Singapore. Published Aug 24, 2026, 05:00 AM Updated Aug 25, 2026, 01:50 PM SINGAPORE – Deep in the Central Catchment Nature Reserve, shiny black beetles roll animal dung for their food and nests, and some navigate with the light of the Milky Way. New research has proven that dung beetles not only help to break down animal faeces, but that their unusual diet can also give clues about the elusive mammals and birds that roam the forests. These tiny but mighty insects can help to fortify biodiversity surveys that currently rely on camera traps, and assess the health of forests. Between January and March 2023, an NTU team led by associate professor Eleanor Slade and research fellow Ong Xin Rui placed 100 traps made of plastic bottles and disposable plates on the forest floor and canopies across 50 sites in the Central Catchment Nature Reserve – Singapore’s largest green lung. Ong Xin Rui (left) and Eleanor Slade preparing a trap using plastic bottles and disposable plates at one of the 50 sites of the Central Catchment Nature Reserve. Slade is holding bait made of human faeces wrapped in a thin cloth, to attract dung beetles to the trap. To lure scuttling dung beetles into the traps, the scientists placed a bundle of human faeces, wrapped in cloth, at each trap. Harnessing their strong sense of smell, dung beetles are particularly drawn to human waste. Each trap was left in the field for 24 hours before the researchers returned to collect the beetles. Tropical dung beetles typically move around 100m a day, stopping to slurp nutrients inside animal droppings. A trap with a plastic bottle dug into the soil to catch dung beetles, and a disposable plate overhead. The bait hangs under the plate to lure the beetles. Slade, who heads the Tropical Ecology and Entomology Lab at NTU’s Asian School of the Environment, said: “The dung beetles will have been flying around and eating dung that’s in the forest, and we’re just using (the bait) to draw them in, and then they land. But their guts are full from what they’ve been eating previously.” Their stomachs would contain a mush of mammal and avian DNA that the scientists sought to identify. Ong said: “The main objective of this study was to draw the interactions between the dung beetles and the types of vertebrate or mammal dung they were feeding on.” More than 540 dung beetles belonging to 14 species were trapped over two months, with the contents of their guts analysed in the lab. A dung beetle from the group Catharsius, found in the Central Catchment Nature Reserve. The team estimates that there are around 25 dung beetle species in Singapore – including those that are new to science. After dissecting the beetles, Ong and her team separated the half-digested materials from their stomachs and transferred them inside solutions that amplify the DNA of mammals and vertebrates such as birds and frogs . After dissecting the beetle, its gut contents are separated for processing and DNA analysis. The samples were sent to a company that sequenced or mapped the DNA found in the beetles’ guts. A total of 18 animal species were detected through DNA matching, including the elusive sambar deer, Sunda pangolin and Sunda slow loris. Other wildlife detected include the brahminy kite – a bird of prey – and a few squirrel and frog species, such as the black-eyed litter frog. As part of the processing, the contents of the beetle’s gut are transferred to a solution that extracts the DNA. Ong noted: “The ones that jumped out to me were the two frog species. You would think dung beetles would feed on the (waste of) a python or a monitor lizard, not a frog. But there are species of dung beetles that feed on carcasses, or the beetle could have fed on something that ate a frog.” She highlighted how the study can also map food webs. The research findings were published in scientific journal Molecular Ecology Resources. While the Central Catchment Nature Reserve is known to be rich in biodiversity, the study was exciting for the NTU researchers because they demonstrated that dung beetles can be used as a DNA resource for surveying wildlife in tropical forests. While such biodiversity surveys are commonly done through camera traps, the cameras are usually placed on the forest floor, which might miss wildlife residing in the canopy. It may also be difficult to identify the specific species of forest rodents through a camera, and having specific DNA sequences helps, noted Ong , who is also a researcher at the NUS Lee Kong Chian Natural History Museum . Beyond just documenting the types of animals in the forest, the researchers were also able to map the interactions between dung beetles and animals across the forest sites. Slade said: “What happens if you lose some species? Is the resilience in there? The next step in ecological research, for conservation, is to look just beyond counting species to actually looking at how they interact, and that’s not been done a lot in the tropics.” These efforts can help to measure the ecological value of a forested area that is planned for development, or track how a degraded forest is improving through conservation projects, she added. Moving forward, the team is looking to test another way of extracting mammals’ DNA from dung beetles without dissecting them. They plan to swab the beetles’ surfaces, such as the mouths and bodies, which potentially contain traces of wildlife DNA, before sending the swabs for DNA analysis. Ash Welch, a nature-based solutions and biodiversity specialist at infrastructure consultancy AECOM, said the NTU research shows the effectiveness of emerging sampling techniques, giving consultants the grounding to adopt them alongside traditional survey methods. In environmental assessments, what tends to be lacking is an in-depth understanding of ecological networks and the interactions that occur within an ecosystem, he added. Knowing about these is important, he said, because ecosystems can provide benefits such as urban cooling against heat and soak up planet-warming greenhouse gases. “That matters because a species list tells you only what is present. A network tells you whether the system is actually working,” said Welch. While the research is clear, using dung beetles for surveys needs to be adopted by frameworks that govern environmental impact assessments, he added. Shabana Begum is a correspondent, with a focus on environment and science, at The Straits Times.

title: Train and bus users will have reminders to keep Singapore clean in Public Hygiene Council campaign
article_text: Participants at ASEAN U.N.I.T.E on Aug 23 discarding trash after the event. Published Aug 23, 2026, 01:55 PM Updated Aug 26, 2026, 02:45 PM SINGAPORE – Public transport users will be reminded to help keep Singapore clean as part of the Public Hygiene Council’s (PHC) 2026 campaign. A Keep Singapore Clean-themed train on the North East Line will be launched in September. Decals covering the interior of all train cars will carry messages encouraging everyone to play his or her role to keep the country clean. Public transport was chosen as the avenue for the new campaign due to the high footfall it receives daily, said PHC’s executive director Christina Liew, who made the announcement on Aug 23. Later in 2026, the messages will also be carried on 10 public buses plying different routes across Singapore. “So, every day, whether it’s the young or old, or anybody in between, it will reach everyone who takes public transport,” Liew said. She was speaking at the second ASEAN U.N.I.T.E (yoU aNd I Together Everytime) held at Punggol Coast Digital Village. ASEAN U.N.I.T.E is PHC’s initiative that brings together diverse communities residing in Singapore, while promoting environmental stewardship through clean and sustainable practices. The event on Aug 23 saw over 400 participants from Brunei Darussalam, Cambodia, Myanmar, Philippines, Thailand and Timor-Leste taking part in a community clean-up and cultural performances. Ambassadors from those countries at the event were also present as environmental advocates to amplify the cleanliness message within their respective communities. The Keep Singapore Clean 2026 campaign was launched in April, with a 30-second video screened across malls reminding shoppers to bin takeaway cups and dispose of food packaging. To mark PHC’s 15th anniversary, it organised a roving exhibition with interactive stations tracing its history, and also launched the Cleanliness Champions Relay, where 20 schools and companies took turns to organise clean-up activities around Singapore. The first leg of the relay was held at Kent Ridge Park on April 19, with subsequent activities planned in areas including Newton, Choa Chu Kang, Sengkang, West Coast Park and East Coast Park. In May, PHC launched a community wall mural at Little India MRT station, made up of photos of PHC’s partners from town councils and grassroots organisations , as part of the Keep Singapore Clean campaign. Addressing the attendees at the Aug 23 event, Senior Parliamentary Secretary for Sustainability and the Environment Goh Hanyan said good public hygiene and cleanliness is key to building a cleaner, healthier and more liveable environment. An example of this was how members of the public returned their food trays and properly disposed of rubbish during the Covid-19 pandemic . First-time PHC volunteer Iveca Cale Villalon Ignacio echoed similar views. The 35-year-old, who has been working as a nurse in Singapore for the past decade, said she became a volunteer with PHC as public hygiene is an important issue to her. Ignacio , who also performed two songs at the event, said she was open to participating in more clean-up activities in the future: “As a healthcare worker, I’m very interested in infection control and public hygiene. If there’s no public hygiene, we would have more patients in the hospital.”

title: Tuas Power to build hydrogen-ready power plant by 2031
article_text: The energy regulator forecasts that Singapore’s peak electricity demand is expected to grow by between 2.4 per cent and 4.8 per cent annually over the next 10 years. Published Aug 20, 2026, 05:00 PM Updated Aug 21, 2026, 02:17 PM SINGAPORE – A hydrogen-ready natural gas power plant to be built by local electricity generator Tuas Power is slated to begin operations in 2031. The combined cycle gas turbine (CCGT) facility – which will be housed in Tuas Power Station – will have a capacity of 670MW, enough to power up to about 1.2 million four-room flats a year. The plant can burn up to 30 per cent hydrogen – a cleaner fuel – with natural gas making up the rest, to generate electricity. It can also use diesel as a back-up fuel when needed. The Energy Market Authority (EMA) announced on Aug 20 that Tuas Power had won the right to build, own and operate a new CCGT generating unit. This came after the authority in April called for energy companies to build up to three new hydrogen-compatible power plants in 2031 and 2032 to help meet Singapore’s future electricity needs. With this award, there will be at least 11 hydrogen-ready natural gas power plants in Singapore by 2032, including four that were completed in 2025. Tuas Power said on Aug 20 that the new plant will not only help to meet Singapore’s growing electricity demand, but also replace ageing generators that are due to retire over the next decade. The plant is scheduled to start operating by December 2031, it added. When asked about the cost of the facility, Tuas Power’s chief operating officer Michael Wong said that the industry benchmark for such a facility is between $700 million and $1 billion. The final cost will be subject to tender outcomes. From 2024, all new and repowered natural gas power plants need to be 10 per cent more efficient and be able to draw on at least 30 per cent hydrogen, when the low-carbon energy source becomes viable in the future. Hydrogen is considered a clean fuel, as it does not produce any CO2 when burned. Natural gas, on the other hand, is a fossil fuel. Singapore’s electricity demand is expected to grow rapidly over the next several years, driven by strong economic growth and transport electrification as well as the expansion of energy-intensive sectors such as semiconductor manufacturing and data centres, said EMA in a statement. The energy regulator forecasts that Singapore’s peak electricity demand is expected to grow by between 2.4 per cent and 4.8 per cent annually over the next 10 years. Peak demand refers to the highest amount of electricity used in a specific period, much like the “rush hour” of power used. By 2031, the peak demand is projected to reach between 9.6 gigawatt (GW) and 11.4 GW. Singapore’s peak demand in 2025 was around 8GW. The call for new power plants in April came after four back-up power units were completed in 2025. Also known as fast-start plants, they are designed to kick-start within minutes if there is a sudden shortfall in power supply. Electricity retailer PacificLight Power completed its two 50MW back-up units in June 2025, and EMA subsidiary Meranti Power launched its two 340MW fast-start units in October 2025. Keppel launched its 600MW hydrogen-compatible plant in May while Sembcorp is expected to launch its 600MW hydrogen-compatible plant in 2026. YTL PowerSeraya is slated to build its 600MW hydrogen-compatible plant by 2027, followed by PacificLight Power’s 670MW facility which is scheduled for 2029. Chin Hui Shan is a journalist covering the environment beat at The Straits Times.

title: Disasters know no borders; climate change escalation requires shared ASEAN response: Edwin Tong
article_text: Minister for Law and Second Minister for Home Affairs Edwin Tong speaking at the ASEAN Strategic Policy Dialogue on Disaster Management 2026 on Aug 19. Published Aug 19, 2026, 10:50 AM Updated Aug 19, 2026, 09:09 PM SINGAPORE – Climate change is intensifying the frequency and severity of natural disasters, and building resilience is no longer optional, said Minister for Law and Second Minister for Home Affairs Edwin Tong. He added that such disasters also know no borders, making solidarity and collective action in ASEAN critical. Tong was speaking at the ASEAN Strategic Policy Dialogue on Disaster Management 2026 held at Parkroyal Collection Marina Bay on Aug 19. The 11th edition of the event was co-organised by the Singapore Civil Defence Force, the ASEAN Secretariat, and the ASEAN Coordinating Centre for Humanitarian Assistance on disaster management. The event saw some 200 government officials, academics and practitioners present, including representatives from ASEAN countries, the European Union, Canada and New Zealand. In his opening speech, Tong said 2026 marked the 10th anniversary of the One ASEAN One Response declaration. He said the declaration had set out a clear ambition to increase the speed, scale and solidarity of ASEAN’s response to any disaster, recognising that an effective response cannot rest on any single institution or mechanism alone. He said: “Yet, even as we have strengthened our capabilities, the challenges we face have also grown. They’ve in fact intensified. Natural disasters have worsened in both scale as well as frequency, and in many ways also its unpredictability.” At the start of his speech, Tong extended his condolences to Indonesia, which experienced a 7.7-magnitude earthquake off the coast of Flores Island on Aug 15. Thousands have been displaced, and at least 53 people were killed. Rescue efforts are ongoing. Attendees at the dialogue observed a moment of silence for the victims of the disaster during a speech by Raditya Jati, Indonesia’s Deputy Minister for Systems and Strategy at the National Disaster Management Authority. Tong also extended his condolences to the Philippines, which is experiencing the compound effect of tropical cyclones Luis and Maymay and the south-west monsoons . Other ASEAN countries have not been spared. Tong said the earthquake that struck Mandalay in Myanmar on March 28, 2025, was one of the deadliest disasters of the year, affecting Thailand and Vietnam as well. He also mentioned Cyclone Senyar , which brought widespread devastation across Indonesia, Thailand and Malaysia. A key concern is the warning earlier in 2026 by the World Meteorological Organization of a super El Nino . Tong said this could mean more severe heatwaves and droughts with serious consequences for food security and public health in South-east Asia. He said: “These events remind us that natural disasters do not at all respect national boundaries, national borders – they are regional challenges that demand regional solutions. “As climate change continues to intensify the frequency and severity of natural disasters across our region and elsewhere in the world, building resilience and depth is no longer optional. “In fact, I believe it is an imperative. It is a must-do.” Tong said Singapore will take up the ASEAN chairmanship in 2027, and it intends to deepen collective preparedness and resilience on several fronts. This includes the hosting of the 10th ASEAN Regional Disaster Emergency Response Simulation Exercise, which will test and validate regional disaster response procedures and coordination. Singapore will also advance ASEAN’s climate and environmental agenda, having designated 2026 as the Year of Climate Adaptation, and is developing a national adaptation plan , underpinned by a $40 million commitment to create a climate-ready nation. Tong said that beyond preparedness, collective action is also essential, and can be extended beyond ASEAN. He said: “We must move beyond reactive responses alone, and embed anticipatory thinking into the foundations, into the very core of our approach to disaster management. “I believe that ASEAN is well-placed to build on its strong foundations to advance the implementation of One ASEAN, One Response initiatives, and eventually extend our collective capabilities to the broader international community.” David Sun is The Straits Times’ crime correspondent. He has a background in criminology and is a licensed private investigator. Humanitarian aid/Disaster relief

title: 76% of coral reefs in Indo-Pacific at risk of drowning from rising seas in coming decades: NTU study
environment_keywords: environment, carbon emissions, greenhouse gas, pollution, conservation, ecosystem, flood, sea level rise
article_text: Coral reefs from the Indo-Pacific. Most corals will not be able to keep pace with the waters if sea level rise exceeds 5.3mm per year, a threshold that can be surpassed by the 2060s if greenhouse gas emissions continue to rise rapidly. Published Aug 18, 2026, 06:45 PM Updated Aug 21, 2026, 02:18 PM SINGAPORE – Three-quarters of coral reefs in the Indo-Pacific region, which includes Singapore, could drown as sea levels rise , a study by Nanyang Technological University (NTU) has found. Most corals will not be able to keep pace with the waters if sea level rise exceeds 5.3mm per year, a threshold that can be surpassed by the 2060s if greenhouse gas emissions continue to rise rapidly. As at 2023 , global sea level rise had been around 4.5mm per year, according to NASA. As Riovie Ramos, the study’s first author and research fellow at NTU’s Earth Observatory of Singapore put it, rising sea level is not the first enemy of coral reefs. Longer-term sea level rise compounds the threats the underwater gardens already face because of construction works at coastal areas and bleaching caused by marine heatwaves. The loss of complex reef structures could also reduce the habitats available to fish. Although coral reefs are submerged, if sea levels rise faster than a reef’s growth, the reef will sit under progressively deeper water, a process scientists call reef drowning. Deeper waters tend to cut off sunlight, and the survival of corals is highly dependent on the amount of light available. In Singapore, corals already live in murky waters, and any further reduction in light reaching them can be dangerous. The loss of complex reef structures could also reduce the habitats available to fish and other marine animals, affecting fisheries, tourism and communities that depend on reefs for food and income, said NTU in a statement on Aug 18. Kyle Morgan, an assistant professor at NTU’s Asian School of the Environment who led the research, said: “Reefs will become progressively submerged. They may still contain living corals, but they will no longer function in the same way, potentially allowing greater wave energy to reach the coastline and increasing (flood) risks to coastal communities.” The study was done by tracing the histories of 288 ancient reef cores from 92 sites across the Indo-Pacific, including the Great Barrier Reef in Australia, Maldives and the Coral Triangle, one of the most biodiverse marine areas in the world spanning the waters of South-east Asia and the Solomon Islands. Reef cores are metres-long cylinders of rock drilled from the reef base, made up of calcium carbonate. They preserve entire past coral histories. By calculating the dates of different sections of a core, scientists can reconstruct how reefs have built up over thousands of years and how the types of corals living on them have changed through time. The NTU researchers calculated the coral fossils’ vertical growth rate across 11,700 years, which is the current geological era after the last ice age. These were done by scouring existing research and by studying some cores collected by the researchers. Assistant professor Kyle Morgan and research fellow Riovie Ramos examining a reef core. Reef cores from Singapore were not included in the study. To make future projections, the researchers identified the highest growth rate each reef achieved in the past and compared them to future sea level rise scenarios, said Ramos. “Under the high-emissions scenario, the sea is projected to rise faster than 76 per cent of the studied reefs can grow, meaning they will likely be inundated by 2100,” added Ramos. Thousands of years ago during the early Holocene period, reefs were often in a high growth state, allowing them to keep up with sea level rise. “Today, reefs face repeated bleaching, ocean acidification, pollution and other stressors which reduce their ability to produce carbonate materials needed for vertical growth,” she noted. The study’s findings were published in scientific journal Nature Communications in August. The researchers also found that the changing landscape of coral reefs, with an increasing share of weedy species, could speed up reef drowning. Weedy species are small, fast-growing corals that can settle on disturbed reefs, but are poor at growing upwards, at 1.9mm a year. “Weedy species are just like weeds on land – they grow fast and cover reef quickly but don’t provide meaningful structure or habitat,” said Morgan. Ancient reefs, on the other hand, were made up of competitive, branching corals that grew upwards the fastest, at 4mm a year. Conservation and reef restoration efforts cannot fully compensate for coral loss if sea levels continue accelerating, added NTU. A 2023 study led by NUS marine biologist Huang Danwei found that in a high carbon emissions scenario, up to 10 per cent of Singapore’s corals could perish. “These dead corals will not be able to contribute to future reef (growth) and thus further impact coral reef persistence over the next century,” said Huang, an associate professor and deputy head of the NUS Lee Kong Chian Natural History Museum. Commenting on the NTU study, he said conservation efforts must be tailored to local reef conditions, which include water quality and the movement of water and sediments. Stressing that the water quality of reefs should be improved, he said: “Allowing reefs to naturally recruit landward as sea levels rise would also reduce the overall loss of reef habitats. “Unless emissions are meaningfully curbed and coral reefs actively managed, the processes that build coral reefs and the vital ecosystem services they provide will remain in jeopardy.” Shabana Begum is a correspondent, with a focus on environment and science, at The Straits Times.

title: Food scientist who turned soya pulp into food among 14 recipients of Singapore eco award
article_text: To squeeze value out of leftover soya pulp that would otherwise go to waste, food scientist Heng Kiang Soon developed ways to turn it into ingredients for human food and agricultural use, among other products. Published Aug 18, 2026, 08:25 PM Updated Aug 18, 2026, 10:32 PM SINGAPORE – To squeeze value out of leftover soya pulp that would otherwise go to waste, food scientist Heng Kiang Soon developed ways to turn it into ingredients for human food and agricultural use, among other products. The pulp, called okara, which is generated after producing soya milk and tofu, is rich in protein and fibre, but it is indigestible by humans and often discarded . Determined to maximise “every resource we already have” in a resource-scarce country like Singapore , Heng developed a technology to make the ingredient soluble and turn it into 14 food and agricultural products like soya cheese, soya cream soup and plant boosters. The plant boosters, which are known as biostimulants, can enhance crop yield and quality. Some of these products have been licensed for commercialisation, said the specialist in food innovation and lecturer at Republic Polytechnic’s School of Applied Science. On Aug 18, Heng was among 14 people presented with the EcoFriend award, which recognises individuals from the private and public sectors, educational institutions, grassroots and non-governmental organisations for their significant contributions to making Singapore more sustainable. He estimated that the production of plant boosters as well as soya cheese, instead of using commercial raw materials, could have substantial cost savings. Converting by-products like this into useful products is not only environmentally friendly, but can also help to generate new business opportunities and build stronger food system resilience, said Heng, who grew up on a farm in Malaysia. “If we learn to see waste not as something to throw away but as a resource with untapped potential, we can unlock solutions that benefit both society and the environment,” added the 50-year-old, who is also looking to recycle other food waste like spent coffee grounds and fruit pulp. Organised by the National Environment Agency, the 17th edition of the biennial EcoFriend Awards was held at National Gallery Singapore. Minister for Sustainability and the Environment Grace Fu, who gave out the awards, said: “Their initiatives have strengthened community networks, encouraged resourcefulness and galvanised action to keep our shared spaces clean, green and resilient.” A total of 510 individuals were nominated for the award, said Fu, with nominations exceeding 500 for the first time in more than a decade. She noted that this points to a sustained and growing interest in environmental sustainability. In her speech, she also mentioned Arunraj Chidambaram, who leads a weekly food rescue initiative in Zhenghua in Bukit Panjang, saving and redistributing 100kg to 200kg of surplus produce each week. Arunraj Chidambaram leads a weekly food rescue initiative in Zhenghua in Bukit Panjang, saving and redistributing 100kg to 200kg of surplus produce each week. Since launching the initiative in 2022, his project has grown from eight to 10 volunteers serving fewer than 60 residents to a weekly operation supported by 20 to 30 volunteers that now reaches over 150 residents in each session. Arunraj, who is the chairman of the Zhenghua Youth Network, said he finds it most rewarding when volunteers get others to join the initiative. “There are bigger environmental problems to be solved. Exposure to activities like food rescue or litter-picking is a gateway for youth to open their minds and start thinking about solutions to other problems with their creative ways,” said the 31-year-old. Boston Pek and some schoolmates from Westwood Primary School designed a robot vacuum cleaner using recycled and repurposed materials. The youngest award recipient in 2026 is 13-year-old Boston Pek. He and some schoolmates from Westwood Primary School designed a robot vacuum cleaner using repurposed materials, including recycled plastic, to help the school’s cleaners. The remote-control-operated vacuum cleaner picks up small items like crumpled paper. “I wanted to make this so that it can ease (the cleaners’) workload while helping to keep the environment clean,” said Boston, who is now studying at Juying Secondary School. Another award recipient is Dazhong Primary School teacher Ong Xuan Wan, who created an experiential learning platform to spark her pupils’ curiosity about science and sustainability. The platform features eco-trails and Pokemon-inspired mascots that guide pupils through hands-on learning to find out more about the fauna and flora in the school, as well as how to recycle, among other topics. “Our environment belongs to the next generation. It is their belief and actions that will decide the future of Singapore and how well we care for our environment,” said the 39-year-old. “I want to plant a seed in every pupil so that it will remind them of the impact of their action or inaction when they grow up.” Chin Hui Shan is a journalist covering the environment beat at The Straits Times. Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment

title: NTU retrofits building to prevent fatal bird collisions
article_text: Published Aug 16, 2026, 05:00 AM Updated Aug 16, 2026, 08:08 PM SINGAPORE – After years of advocacy by students, a Nanyang Technological University (NTU) building has undergone a critical makeover to prevent fatal bird collisions as the academic year begins this August. Since the completion of the School of Art, Design and Media (ADM) building in 2006, students have watched scores of birds crash into the gleaming building on the fringe of the forested Western Water Catchment. These range from the yellow-rumped flycatcher to the black-backed dwarf kingfisher to the Japanese sparrowhawk. This happened because the birds struggled to differentiate the reflective windows from the surroundings. While the lucky ones survived the impact, the less fortunate succumbed to their injuries or drowned in a reflecting pool in the building’s courtyard. Their deaths are part of a worldwide problem as urbanisation creeps into natural habitats. Annually, millions of bird s die from striking buildings worldwide. In Singapore, collision with man-made structures was named the top culprit of bird mortality cases logged since 2020. At NTU, a student-led initiative named Project Avigate was launched in 2022 to reduce these fatalities, with students and alumni calling for the installation of anti-collision decals on the ADM building. Made possible by $119,009.92 in joint funding from a Project Avigate fund-raiser and NTU, the patterned decals now cover about 800 sq m of the most dangerous glass panels identified by students. The installation of the decals, a process that took a month, ended on July 31. The patterns remain largely invisible from a distance, preserving the building’s aesthetic facade, said a School of ADM spokesperson. Installed ahead of the annual southward migratory season, when birds arrive in Singapore to flee winter in the Northern Hemisphere , the decals are expected to last about seven years. The School of ADM spokesperson said there are no plans to apply decals to other parts of the school, as addressing the identified flight path resolves the primary area of concern for collisions. Project Avigate co-founder Tang Kean Seng described the installation as “absolutely incredible and surreal”. It marked the culmination of four years’ worth of patrols, documentation and a fund-raising campaign that secured $60,000 from the public – double the target set by the university, said Tang. The rest of the project’s cost was covered by NTU. This built on the efforts of several batches of seniors, who had raised awareness of the issue nearly 10 years ago, according to Tang. The patterns remain largely invisible from a distance, preserving the building’s aesthetic facade. He said: “Institutional change takes time, but with more concerned and informed voices, we can build a constructive environment to accelerate the process.” He added that the team was pleased to observe that the decals had limited impact on the building’s aesthetic. Tang noted that some $36,000 remaining after the decal installation will support future education, outreach, research and maintenance. This includes buying patrol and monitoring equipment – such as gloves and containers – which was previously funded by member donations. Moving forward, Tang said the Project Avigate team will prioritise monitoring the effectiveness of the decals. They hope their findings will inform broader anti-collision strategies across Singapore, with Tang noting that they have already received encouraging queries from members of the public hoping to learn from their experience. Installers from Jestac putting up 3M customised printing film (collision-preventive decals) on the facade of NTU’s School of Art, Design and Media building. Meanwhile, Jestac, the contractor which installed the decals, said it has observed an increase in inquirie s about anti-bird strike film since 2022, when the National Parks Board released guidelines for making buildings safer for birds . Jestac marketing manager Angelia Kay said the film is generally recommended for properties surrounded by significant greenery and featuring large, highly reflective glass facades, as these conditions significantly increase the likelihood of collisions. While awareness is growing, Kay noted that overall adoption of the film remains relatively limited. She declined to specify which other properties in the country have installed the material. Tang said : “We once again call for the wider society, especially estate and building managers, to treat bird-window collisions seriously, and it would be our absolute pleasure to share our expertise and experience if anyone is considering retrofitting their building. “For architects and developing agencies, we urge them to be extra mindful of future building designs, especially given Singapore’s greening efforts within even the urban centre.”

title: Keep on swimming: 42 critically endangered hawksbill turtles released off Sisters’ Islands
article_text: A total of 42 hawksbill turtle hatchlings were released off Sisters’ Islands Marine Park on Aug 13 and 14. Published Aug 14, 2026, 05:45 PM Updated Aug 18, 2026, 06:11 PM SINGAPORE – A hawksbill turtle in June laid 97 eggs perilously close to the waterline on Big Sister’s Island, leaving its nest vulnerable to being flooded by high tides. But with a little help from the National Parks Board (NParks), 42 tenacious hatchlings made it out of their shells and stroked their way into the waters off Sisters’ Islands on Aug 13 and 14. To protect the unhatched turtles, the eggs were retrieved by NParks when they were about six weeks old and moved to the turtle hatchery on Small Sister’s Island. Established in 2018, the hatchery provides a conducive environment for turtle eggs to incubate, hatch safely and make it out to sea. The eggs were not relocated earlier to avoid stressing the creatures, and to give them more time to develop. This was the third clutch to hatch at Sisters’ Islands Marine Park in 2026. As at Aug 14, 294 turtle hatchlings have emerged from the hatchery, said NParks. There have also been 59 sightings of live sea turtles, and 25 nests recorded for the 2026 nesting season. Hawksbill turtles, named for their powerful beak-like mouth s , typically visit Singapore’s shores between May and October to lay their eggs. The hawksbill is one of two species of marine turtles that can be found in Singapore waters ; the other is the green turtle. The hatch rate of about 43 per cent for the latest clutch is unusual, said Collin Tong, deputy director of the coastal and marine branch of NParks’ National Biodiversity Centre. The previous clutch that hatched last week had a hatch rate of almost 88 per cent, and the average hatch rate is about 70 per cent, he noted. “Based on the various signs, we can see that possibly this is an inexperienced mother because she laid (the eggs) very low, and the low egg count is likely that she’s a young mother,” he said. A female turtle usually lays about 100 to 150 eggs at a time, he added. After emerging from the nest, the hatchlings were assessed, with their weight and number of scutes (scales) recorded, for instance, to determine their health status and for research purposes. Emerging from the nest is just the start of a hatchling’s test of endurance. Many are eaten by predators like shorebirds , become disoriented by artificial light, become accidentally entangled in rubbish, or fall prey to poachers in the open sea. The release of the hawksbill turtle hatchlings off Sisters’ Islands Marine Park on Aug 14. Hawksbill turtles, which are critically endangered, take roughly two decades to mature, and females return to nest on beaches near where they hatched. One female turtle, affectionately called Dorothy by NParks staff, has been returning to Singapore’s shores time and again at the peak of the 2026 sea turtle nesting season, attempting to nest. After Dorothy made two failed attempts to lay her eggs at East Coast Park on June 22 and July 10, NParks’ group director for the National Biodiversity Centre Karenne Tun told The Straits Times that there have been two more reported sightings of her attempts on July 15 and Aug 7. These failures were likely because of an injured hind flipper which hindered her ability to nest . Separately, NParks on Aug 4 relocated a new clutch of 92 hawksbill turtle eggs from East Coast Park to the hatchery, where they will have a higher chance of survival away from human activity, light pollution and predators. After emerging from the nest, the hatchlings were assessed, with their weight and number of scutes (scales) recorded, for instance, to determine their health status and for research purposes. On helping to increase the chances of hawksbill turtles surviving, Tong said: “I definitely feel very happy. It’s like being a proud father. Hopefully I will get to see them in 30 years’ time when they return.” While collaborative work to help Singapore’s sea turtles has been ongoing for nearly two decades, NParks initiated a programme in 2016 to conserve the two native turtle species, both of which are at high risk of extinction. The other species, the green turtle, has been spotted in local waters but unlike in neighbouring Malaysia, has not been recorded nesting here. As part of the programme, NParks conducts biodiversity beach patrols during nesting season at dawn between 5am and 7am to look for nesting turtles, laid nests and hatchlings. Tun advises members of the public who encounter a nesting turtle on the beach to keep their distance from the turtle and the eggs. This is because touching a turtle can scare or provoke it, and handling the eggs may result in damage or introduction of bacteria into the nest. NParks also on Aug 4 relocated a new clutch of 92 hawksbill turtle eggs from East Coast Park to the hatchery, where they will have a higher chance of survival away from human activity, light pollution and predators. Instead, members of the public can contact the NParks helpline on 1800-476-1600 to report their sighting. Tun said: “They should talk softly and stay out of sight, and not shine lights at the turtle or use flash photography. “Light and noise may scare the turtle and cause it to leave without laying any eggs.” The public should also keep clear of tracks left by the turtles, as researchers use the tracks to identify the species of turtle and to locate nests. Those who are interested in participating in NParks’ efforts to monitor sea turtle populations in Singapore can join NParks’ Biodiversity Beach Patrol through its website. Correction note: The story has been updated with NParks’ correct hotline. Chin Hui Shan is a journalist covering the environment beat at The Straits Times.

title: askST: How worrying is Singapore’s haze outlook, and how can you protect yourself?
environment_keywords: environment, pollution, haze, air quality, forest fires
article_text: Firefighters battling a spreading peat fire in a residential district in Pengerang, Johor, in January. Published Aug 10, 2026, 06:25 PM Updated Aug 11, 2026, 12:40 PM SINGAPORE – Dry conditions that have worsened fires in the region are expected to persist this week, raising the risk of haze over Singapore. On Aug 9, the Republic’s haze task force announced its readiness to roll out plans after the 24-hour Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) entered the moderate range in central Singapore in the afternoon. Following the recent warning of the possible return of hazy weather, The Straits Times looks at what residents need to know to protect themselves. Singapore is among the southern South-east Asian countries at high risk of severe haze affecting the region for the rest of 2026. These conditions are expected to peak from August to September , according to think-tank Singapore Institute of International Affairs. This is due to unusually hot and dry weather, fuelled by an intensifying El Nino climate phenomenon. El Nino occurs when the atmosphere reacts to a sustained warming of the Pacific Ocean’s surface temperatures above average levels, bringing less rain, longer dry spells and higher temperatures to South-east Asia. Scientists have warned that the 2026/2027 El Nino could become a “Godzilla” or Super El Nino , with temperatures in the tropical Pacific warming rapidly. El Nino events tend to have the greatest bearing on Singapore’s rainfall during the dry south-west monsoon season from June to September. Past moderate-to-strong El Nino events over the last 30 years have resulted in 40 per cent to 80 per cent less rainfall in parts of Singapore for some months. These drier and warmer conditions worsen the region’s peatland and forest fires, which are the main drivers for transboundary haze experienced in Singapore. The National Environment Agency (NEA) on Aug 9 said the dry conditions that escalated hot spots in Indonesia’s Sumatra and Kalimantan are expected to persist in the coming week, increasing the risk of haze if the fires persist. Under prevailing southeasterly winds, smoke haze could be carried to Singapore, especially from the hot spots in the southern parts of Sumatra. For 2026, the confluence of El Nino and the potential development of another climate phenomenon called the positive Indian Ocean Dipole could prolong the dry season and extend it into October. A positive Indian Ocean Dipole is similar to El Nino, but develops in the equatorial Indian Ocean. To manage the impact of haze, Singapore set up a task force in 1994 chaired by NEA. The task force, which typically convenes yearly before the dry season starts in June, has already met twice in 2026. The task force will roll out its plans. Air quality enters the unhealthy range when th e 24-hour PSI, derived from the 24-hour average concentration levels of six pollutants, exceeds 100. Once the PSI enters the unhealthy zone between 101 and 200, NEA will issue daily haze advisories to help the public plan their activities for the following day. In such conditions, the elderly, pregnant women and children are advised to minimise prolonged or strenuous outdoor physical activities. People with chronic lung and heart diseases should avoid such activities entirely. Should air quality exceed certain thresholds, outdoor events can be cancelled and schools closed. For example, when the PSI soared to the very unhealthy range in 2015 , primary and secondary schools, special education schools and kindergartens run by the Ministry of Education were closed for a day. An acrid burning smell often accompanies transboundary haze, due to a mixture of gases from forest and peat fires. These pungent gases are different from the air pollutants monitored for air quality. The smell tends to be worse at night when winds are weaker, slowing the dilution and dispersal of pollutants. Cooler temperatures also restrict their upward dispersal. Poor visibility does not necessarily mean the air is more polluted. Lower visibility can be due to the amount of water vapour in the air, as water droplets scatter light. Certain air pollutant particles attract water molecules, creating larger particles that scatter even more light. This means visibility can be much lower on hazy days with high humidity or rain. Occasionally, the smell of burning can be due to localised burning, rather than transboundary haze. Monitor the one-hour PM2.5 readings , which are a key indicator of current air quality during transboundary haze periods. These readings reflect the average concentration of fine particulate matter over the past hour and can fluctuate throughout the day based on weather conditions . There are four bands on the PM2.5 concentration scale: zero to 55 for normal, 56 to 150 for elevated, 151 to 250 for high, and very high for any higher reading. When these readings are at elevated levels, vulnerable individuals – including the elderly, pregnant women and those with chronic lung or heart disease – should avoid all outdoor activities for the next hour. The public can view a personal guide for planning outdoor activities using these readings at this website . N95 masks are not needed for short periods of exposure, such as commuting to work or walking from a bus stop to a shopping centre . These masks are recommended under certain conditions, such as if a healthy person must be outdoors for several hours when the air quality is in the hazardous range, with a PSI reading of over 300. Surgical masks can reduce discomfort caused by haze by acting as a barrier against larger irritant particles, but unlike N95 masks, they are not effective in filtering fine particles. To stay updated, check the NEA website ( nea.gov.sg ), the haze microsite ( haze.gov.sg ) , the myENV app, and the NEA’s social media channels for the latest information . Residents can protect their indoor environment by closing doors and windows to limit haze particles entering the home. Wet-cleaning methods such as mopping and wiping can be used to remove settled dust. Those with air-conditioners that draw unfiltered air from the outside should ensure outdoor air intake openings are closed. Portable air purifiers can help cut indoor particle levels. Opt for purifiers equipped with highly efficient air filters to remove fine particles. More tips can be found at this website . The authorities said national N95 mask stockpiles are sufficient. During one of Singapore’s worst episodes of haze pollution in 2015, vulnerable and needy Singaporeans were able to collect N95 masks from community clubs islandwide. Meteorological Service Singapore

title: Air-con not needed to cool a building
article_text: Office development Paya Lebar Green is one of 50 buildings in Singapore that rely on alternative cooling methods instead of air-conditioning. Published Aug 10, 2026, 05:00 AM Updated Aug 21, 2026, 02:19 PM SINGAPORE – Hotter days on the horizon are set to stretch demand for cooling indoors. Air -conditioning is an energy guzzler that contributes to global warming when it emits planet-warming refrigerants. Cooling alone accounts for 40 per cent to 60 per cent of a commercial building’s total energy use in Singapore. Nearly 50 buildings in Singapore have adopted alternative cooling methods that safeguard workers’ comfort while reducing energy use. Alternative cooling technologies that do not rely solely on air-conditioning can reduce a building’s energy use for cooling by up to 48 per cent. Air-conditioning – set at a higher temperature between 25.5 deg C and 27 deg C – is paired with fans. Fans increase air movement, which helps the body release heat more easily through the skin. Hybrid cooling is the most widely used alternative cooling method as there is no need for major retrofits. To date, 26 buildings have adopted this, including The GEAR, Kajima Corp’s regional headquarters, and Temasek Shophouse. The GEAR uses a mix of methods, including hybrid cooling, natural ventilation and radiant cooling, to achieve a 45 per cent reduction in energy use for cooling. A room can be cooled through panels on its ceiling. Heat naturally moves from warmer objects to cooler surfaces. This system removes heat by circulating chilled water through panels, pipes or surfaces, absorbing heat and keeping temperatures of surfaces below room temperature. A network of pipes carrying chilled water draws heat away to cool the building via radiation and natural convective air movement. Radiant cooling panels attached to a ceiling within The GEAR. Cooling and ventilation are provided through ceiling-mounted systems called active chilled beams. Each beam contains coils that carry chilled water. Fresh air that has been cooled and treated is pushed through small nozzles in the beam. This fast-moving airflow draws warmer air in the room across the cold water coils, cooling it down before the air sinks to reach people in the room. Active chilled beams (far left, top) at L-Acoustics’ office in Paya Lebar Green. A study that the Building and Construction Authority commissioned in 2024 identified that these newer cooling technologies can help high-performing green buildings save up to 80 per cent of their energy use, up from 72 per cent now. This last-mile gap of 8 percentage points calls for technologies that are more novel in nature, or require higher upfront investments, planning and design. Following the study, upcoming office tower The Clifford at Raffles Place will be piloting another cooling method for the building’s retail space. This method is called passive displacement cooling, which involves leveraging the natural rise of warm air. Cooling coils near the ceiling will cool the warm air , which then sinks to the floor. This creates a continuous cycle. This marks the first time such cooling technology is being tested for a retail environment in Singapore. It is more common in office and classrooms elsewhere.

title: Sunda slow loris found in industrial estate near Tuas released after 2 months
article_text: A Sunda slow loris was rescued by the Animal Concerns Research and Education Society from an industrial estate in western Singapore on May 26. Published Aug 09, 2026, 05:00 AM Updated Aug 10, 2026, 05:47 AM SINGAPORE – Workers were surprised to discover a young slow loris peering at them inside an industrial building near Tuas in May. The fuzzy creature was eventually rescued by the Animal Concerns Research and Education Society (ACRES), which identified it as the Sunda slow loris, an endangered venomous primate native to Singapore. This has been the second Sunda slow loris rescued by ACRES so far in 2026. The first was found in the corridor of an HDB block in Sin Ming in January. The case was unusual, as the species’ wild population is confined to the Central Catchment Nature Reserve, said ACRES chief executive Kalaivanan Balakrishnan, adding that the slow loris was first spotted on a tree before it entered the premises. He guessed that the tree-dwelling primate could have accidentally hitched a lift in a lorry or was an abandoned illegal pet. The Sunda slow loris rescued in May was rehabilitated for two months at the ACRES Wildlife Rescue Centre in Jalan Lekar. Fortunately, the animal was only mildly dehydrated upon discovery. Kalaivanan declined to reveal further details about its location, due to the species’ rarity and its popularity in the illegal wildlife trade. “Slow lorises are prominent in the illegal wildlife trade. They are also sadly mistreated and used as photo props in other countries,” he said. It is rare to come across cases involving wild slow lorises due to their shy and elusive nature, said ACRES’ wildlife rescue and rehabilitation manager Karina Lim. However, Lim added: “As more habitat loss occurs, it may result in animals venturing out in search of other suitable green spaces to inhabit.” Notwithstanding the slow loris’ mysterious origins, it was deemed suitable for release, as it did not display any captive behaviours or physical modifications common among illegally kept pets. With bulbous eyes and furry bodies, these slow-moving primates may look like stuffed toys, but their venom-filled bites can rot flesh and cause anaphylactic shock in humans. In the exotic pet trade, poachers typically cut or pull out the animal’s sharp teeth to prevent it from biting its owner. To prepare for the slow loris’ release, a customised rehabilitation plan was developed from reviewing scientific literature and consulting an overseas wildlife rescue organisation with expertise in slow lorises, said Lim. The nocturnal animal was monitored almost nightly and fed a diet including insects, bird eggs and tree sap, much of which had to be sourced naturally, she added. Fluid was also given to resolve signs of stress detected in its blood, possibly the result of being stranded outside of its natural environment, said ACRES’ veterinary department manager Tan Hui Min. Once the staff saw that the slow loris could climb, forage and demonstrate a healthy aversion to humans, they knew that it was time to say goodbye. The Sunda slow loris before it was released in August into a forested area inhabited by wild slow lorises. Said Lim: “We have been rooting for his release from the very start, and we are glad that after two months of rehabilitation efforts, he was able to return and be free in the wild again.” On Aug 3, the primate was released in a forested area populated by fellow wild slow lorises. As Singapore continues to clear its forested areas for developments, ACRES is looking to help wildlife and improve their welfare, said Kalaivanan. “With expansion plans taking shape at ACRES, we are able to do a lot more advanced rehabilitation work which will give both our native and non-native wild animals a better chance back in the wild,” he said. The Sunda slow loris is the only known venomous primate. It produces a yellow secretion from glands on its inner arm, which combines with saliva to deliver a painful bite. Due to illegal demand for slow lorises as pets, all nine o f its species are currently threatened with extinction.

title: S’pore gives conditional nod to import solar power from Malaysia
environment_keywords: environment, decarbonisation, clean energy, solar power
article_text: Singapore aims to import around 6GW of electricity by 2035 – about a third of its energy needs then. Published Aug 07, 2026, 05:00 PM Updated Aug 11, 2026, 12:41 PM SINGAPORE – The Republic could be tapping solar power from Malaysia in its quest for clean energy , with conditional approval given to two companies to import a total of 900 megawatts (MW) of electricity. The projects will supply power generated from solar and battery energy storage systems in Johor, the Energy Market Authority (EMA) said on Aug 7. The batteries will also store electricity generated by solar power. A total of 900MW of imported electricity will be able to meet the electricity demand of one million four-room HDB households annually. The latest tie-up brings the number of electricity import projects granted such approvals and licences to 13, with a combined capacity of 9.25GW. The projects cover solar, wind and hydropower from Malaysia, Indonesia, Cambodia, Vietnam and Australia. Singapore aims to import around 6GW of electricity by 2035 – about a third of its energy needs then. Approval was granted to Sembcorp Utilities for a proposed capacity of 300MW, and Southern Solar Alliance – a wholly-owned subsidiary of Malaysian developer Ditrolic Energy Holdings – for a proposed capacity of 600MW. Both companies are aiming to start commercial operations around 2029, said EMA. They will have to obtain all requisite approvals from relevant jurisdictions, conclude power purchase agreements with buyers, secure sufficient financing and conclude various project development milestones in order to start the projects. In a separate statement, SembCorp Utilities said the project will be supported by a large-scale development at Linggiu Reservoir in Johor, comprising an approximate 2.2GWp floating solar photovoltaic system and up to 4.3GWh of battery energy storage. “Designed to meet energy demand in both Singapore and Malaysia, the project will leverage the existing and future subsea interconnection infrastructure between both countries to facilitate cross-border power flows and strengthen regional energy connectivity,” it added. Independent think-tank Centre for Strategic Energy and Resources’s founding co-chairman Victor Nian said the move helps to ensure that Singapore’s clean energy imports are diverse. Diversifying its power imports could also help Singapore become a regional clean energy trading hub as it gains experience in cross-border electricity trade, he added. A company has to undergo three stages before it is granted an electricity import licence from EMA. The first stage entails the firm getting “conditional approval” from EMA, which means the regulator has found that a project’s proposal is technically and commercially viable. The firm will then begin further surveys and feasibility studies. If it can demonstrate its ability to meet the requirements of both the host country and Singapore, EMA will then award it a conditional licence. At this point, the project will be in an advanced developmental stage. The third and final step is when EMA issues the importer licence. EMA said the approvals build on the strong momentum in bilateral energy cooperation between Singapore and Malaysia. In October 2025, Singapore granted conditional approval to import 1GW of low-carbon electricity – mainly in the form of hydropower – from Sarawak to Singapore. Singapore Energy Interconnections, Tenaga Nasional Berhad and SP Group also signed a Joint Development Agreement to conduct a full feasibility study for a second electricity interconnection of up to 2GW between Singapore and Peninsular Malaysia. The existing interconnection allows up to 1GW of bi-directional electricity flows. Low-carbon electricity imports are a key part of Singapore’s strategy to decarbonise the power sector, which accounts for 40 per cent of the country’s total emissions, said EMA. The authority will continue to engage companies with credible and commercially viable import proposals that can contribute to the decarbonisation of the power sector, it added. Chin Hui Shan is a journalist covering the environment beat at The Straits Times.

title: Renaming MTI to Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry is much more than rebranding, experts say
